disease.name: Hypertension
disease.icd_10_code: I10 (Essential Hypertension); I11 (Hypertensive Heart Disease); I12 (Hypertensive Chronic Kidney Disease); I13 (Hypertensive Heart and Chronic Kidney Disease); I15 (Secondary Hypertension); O10-O16 (Hypertension in Pregnancy)
disease.category: Cardiovascular Disease / Endocrine and Metabolic Disease

overview.description: Hypertension (high blood pressure) is a chronic medical condition in which the force of blood against artery walls is persistently elevated — defined as systolic blood pressure (SBP) ≥140 mmHg and/or diastolic blood pressure (DBP) ≥90 mmHg on repeated measurements (WHO/ESH/ESC definition), or ≥130/80 mmHg by ACC/AHA 2017 guidelines. Often called the 'silent killer', hypertension causes no symptoms in the majority of patients until severe or life-threatening complications — such as heart attack, stroke, heart failure, or kidney failure — develop. It is the single most important modifiable risk factor for global cardiovascular mortality.
overview.affected_organ: Arteries and blood vessels throughout the body; primary target organs: Heart, Brain, Kidneys, Eyes, and Peripheral blood vessels
overview.prevalence: Approximately 1.28 billion adults aged 30-79 worldwide have hypertension (WHO 2023); only 42% are diagnosed and treated; affects 1 in 3 adults globally. Responsible for 10.8 million deaths annually.
overview.age_group: Prevalence increases with age; affects all age groups including children and adolescents; >70% of adults over 70 years are hypertensive.

blood_pressure_classification.measurement_method: Average of ≥2 readings on ≥2 separate occasions; patient seated, quiet for 5 minutes; correct cuff size; no caffeine/exercise/smoking 30 min before
blood_pressure_classification.note: ACC/AHA 2017 guidelines define hypertension at ≥130/80 mmHg; ESH/ESC 2018 and WHO define it at ≥140/90 mmHg. Indian guidelines (API/CSI) align with ESH/ESC (≥140/90 mmHg). Clinician should follow national guidelines.

types.name: Primary (Essential) Hypertension
types.description: The most common form — accounting for 90-95% of all hypertension. No single identifiable cause. Results from complex interplay of genetic predisposition, age-related vascular stiffening, lifestyle factors (high sodium intake, obesity, physical inactivity, excess alcohol), and neurohormonal dysregulation (overactive renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, sympathetic nervous system overactivity).
types.common_in: Adults over 40; family history; overweight individuals; high sodium diet populations
types.note: Cannot be cured but effectively managed with lifestyle changes and medication

types.name: Secondary Hypertension
types.description: Hypertension caused by an identifiable, potentially treatable underlying condition. Accounts for 5-10% of all hypertension cases. Should be actively screened for in: young patients (<30 years) with hypertension, resistant hypertension (BP uncontrolled on ≥3 drugs), sudden onset or worsening hypertension, and hypertension with associated clinical clues.
common_causes: Chronic Kidney Disease (most common secondary cause — 3-4%)
Renovascular Hypertension — renal artery stenosis (atherosclerotic or fibromuscular dysplasia)
Primary Hyperaldosteronism (Conn's Syndrome) — most common endocrine cause; hypokalemia is a clue
Pheochromocytoma — paroxysmal hypertension with headache, sweating, palpitations triad
Cushing's Syndrome — cortisol excess; central obesity, purple striae, buffalo hump
Obstructive Sleep Apnoea — very common; unrefreshing sleep, snoring, daytime somnolence
Hyperthyroidism — high output state; wide pulse pressure
Coarctation of the Aorta — elevated BP in arms, low BP in legs; radio-femoral delay
Drug-induced — NSAIDs, oral contraceptive pills, decongestants, steroids, calcineurin inhibitors (ciclosporin), cocaine, amphetamines
types.common_in: Young adults with uncontrolled BP; patients with resistant hypertension

types.name: White Coat Hypertension
types.description: Blood pressure elevated in a clinical setting (doctor's office) but normal on ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) or home BP monitoring. Due to anxiety response to medical environment. May have lower cardiovascular risk than sustained hypertension but higher risk than true normotension — monitoring warranted.
types.diagnosis: Office BP ≥140/90 + ABPM daytime average <135/85 mmHg
types.management: Lifestyle modification; regular follow-up; ABPM every 1-2 years; antihypertensives generally not required unless high cardiovascular risk

types.name: Masked Hypertension
types.description: Normal blood pressure in clinic but elevated on ambulatory or home monitoring. Particularly dangerous — often missed; carries cardiovascular risk similar to sustained hypertension. More common in smokers, physically active individuals measured at rest, and those with stress-related BP elevation during daily activities.
types.diagnosis: Office BP <140/90 + ABPM daytime average ≥135/85 mmHg
types.management: Antihypertensive therapy as for sustained hypertension; ABPM essential for diagnosis

types.name: Isolated Systolic Hypertension (ISH)
types.description: Systolic BP ≥140 mmHg with normal diastolic BP (<90 mmHg). Most common form of hypertension in elderly (>65 years). Caused by age-related loss of arterial elasticity (arteriosclerosis), resulting in a wide pulse pressure. Increased pulse pressure increases risk of stroke, MI, and heart failure even more than both systolic and diastolic elevation.
types.management: Antihypertensive therapy; calcium channel blockers and thiazide diuretics preferred; caution with lowering BP too aggressively in very elderly (J-curve phenomenon)

types.name: Isolated Diastolic Hypertension
types.description: Diastolic BP ≥90 mmHg with normal systolic BP (<140 mmHg). More common in younger adults. Results from increased peripheral vascular resistance with maintained aortic compliance. Associated with increased cardiovascular risk.
types.management: Lifestyle modification first; antihypertensives if persistent or high overall cardiovascular risk

types.name: Resistant Hypertension
types.description: BP remaining above target (≥140/90 mmHg) despite adherence to a full-dose, optimally tolerated three-drug regimen including a diuretic, or BP controlled on four or more drugs. True resistant hypertension (after excluding pseudo-resistance from white coat effect, poor adherence, and suboptimal therapy) affects ~10-15% of treated hypertensives. Mandatory secondary cause screen.
types.management: Screen for secondary causes; optimize existing drugs; add spironolactone (4th drug) — most effective; renal denervation (investigational)

types.name: Hypertensive Crisis
types.description: Severe elevation of BP (usually >180/120 mmHg) requiring immediate assessment. Divided into: (a) Hypertensive Urgency — severe BP without acute target organ damage; oral medications and gradual BP reduction over 24-48 hours; and (b) Hypertensive Emergency — severe BP WITH acute target organ damage (aortic dissection, pulmonary oedema, hypertensive encephalopathy, acute MI, acute stroke, eclampsia, acute renal failure, MAHA). Emergency requires immediate IV therapy in ICU.
types.urgency_management: Oral antihypertensives; BP reduced gradually over 24-48 hours; no rapid reduction
types.emergency_management: ICU admission; IV antihypertensives; organ-specific treatment; controlled BP reduction (10-20% in first hour; 25% within 24 hours for most; specific protocols for aortic dissection and stroke)

types.name: Hypertension in Pregnancy
types.description: Includes: Chronic Hypertension (pre-existing before 20 weeks), Gestational Hypertension (new onset after 20 weeks without proteinuria), Preeclampsia (HTN ≥140/90 after 20 weeks WITH proteinuria ≥300mg/24h or other end-organ involvement), Eclampsia (preeclampsia with seizures), and HELLP Syndrome (Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets). Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy affect 10% of pregnancies and are a leading cause of maternal and perinatal mortality worldwide.
types.management: Methyldopa, Labetalol, Nifedipine (sustained release) are safe in pregnancy; ACE inhibitors and ARBs are ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED; IV Magnesium Sulfate for eclampsia seizure prevention

severity_levels.name: High Normal Blood Pressure
severity_levels.risk: Increased cardiovascular risk; not treated with drugs unless high overall CV risk; lifestyle modification essential
severity_levels.management: Lifestyle modification; repeat measurement in 6 months; treat hypertension risk factors (obesity, dyslipidemia, diabetes)

severity_levels.name: Grade 1 (Mild) Hypertension
severity_levels.risk: Moderate cardiovascular risk; risk significantly elevated if combined with other CV risk factors
severity_levels.target_organ_damage: Possible early changes — mild LVH, microalbuminuria
severity_levels.management: Lifestyle modification + single antihypertensive drug (ACEi OR ARB OR CCB OR thiazide diuretic); reassess in 1-3 months

severity_levels.name: Grade 2 (Moderate) Hypertension
severity_levels.symptoms: Headache more common; dizziness; visual blurring possible
severity_levels.management: Combination antihypertensive therapy (2 drugs) from outset; lifestyle modification; reassess in 1 month; screen for end-organ damage

severity_levels.name: Grade 3 (Severe) Hypertension
severity_levels.symptoms: Headache, visual disturbance, palpitations more likely; nausea
severity_levels.target_organ_damage: LVH, proteinuria, elevated creatinine, retinopathy; established CV disease common
severity_levels.management: Combination antihypertensive therapy (2-3 drugs); urgent assessment for end-organ damage; consider same-day initiation; screen for secondary causes

hypertensive_urgency.definition: Severe BP elevation WITHOUT acute target organ damage
hypertensive_urgency.management: Oral antihypertensives; reduce BP gradually over 24-48 hours; can manage as outpatient with close follow-up

hypertensive_emergency.definition: Severe BP elevation WITH acute target organ damage: hypertensive encephalopathy, acute MI, acute LVF/pulmonary oedema, aortic dissection, eclampsia, acute renal failure, intracranial haemorrhage, MAHA
hypertensive_emergency.symptoms: Severe headache, visual loss, confusion, chest pain, dyspnoea, focal neurology, nausea/vomiting
hypertensive_emergency.management: IMMEDIATE ICU admission; IV antihypertensives; organ-specific protocols; reduce BP by maximum 10-20% in first hour; 25% reduction over 24 hours (EXCEPT aortic dissection — target <120/80 within 20 min; ischaemic stroke — permissive hypertension protocol)

genetic_factors: Polygenic inheritance — family history is a strong independent risk factor; BP heritability estimated 30-60%
Multiple gene variants affecting renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), sodium channel transport, sympathetic nervous system activity
Specific monogenic forms (rare): Liddle's syndrome (constitutively active ENaC sodium channel), Gordon's syndrome, glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism (GRA)
Gene variants affecting sodium reabsorption in kidney tubules (primary defect in renal sodium handling — Guyton's hypothesis)
modifiable_risk_factors: High dietary sodium intake — direct stimulation of RAAS; volume expansion; vascular stiffness; target <2.3g/day (WHO <2g/day)
Obesity and overweight — adipose tissue activates RAAS and sympathetic nervous system; increases cardiac output; adipokine-mediated inflammation
Physical inactivity — reduces vascular endothelial function; increases peripheral vascular resistance
Excessive alcohol consumption (>14 units/week men; >7 units/week women) — raises BP acutely and chronically via sympathetic activation
Smoking — acute vasopressor effect of nicotine; damages vascular endothelium; accelerates atherosclerosis
Chronic psychosocial stress — sustained sympathetic activation; cortisol excess; poor lifestyle behaviours
Unhealthy diet — high saturated fat, low potassium, low calcium, low magnesium intake
Excessive caffeine intake — acute and mild pressor effect; habitual use less significant
non_modifiable_risk_factors: Age — arterial stiffening (arteriosclerosis) with aging; SBP rises with age; DBP peaks at 50-60 then falls
Male sex — higher prevalence of hypertension in men until women enter menopause
Postmenopausal women — loss of oestrogen's vasodilatory and cardioprotective effects
South Asian (Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi) and African/African-American ethnicity — higher salt sensitivity; higher RAAS activity; lower renin hypertension in African populations
pathophysiological_mechanisms: Renal sodium retention — kidney retains excess sodium and water → expanded blood volume → elevated cardiac output → sustained hypertension
RAAS overactivation — excess angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction, sodium retention, and aldosterone release
Sympathetic nervous system overactivity — increased heart rate, cardiac output, and peripheral vascular resistance
Endothelial dysfunction — reduced nitric oxide (NO) production → impaired vasodilation → increased vascular resistance
Arterial stiffness — age-related loss of aortic elasticity → increased pulse wave velocity → isolated systolic hypertension
Chronic low-grade inflammation — inflammatory cytokines damage vessel walls

secondary_hypertension_causes.mechanism: Sodium and water retention; RAAS activation; reduced GFR; proteinuria
Reduced renal blood flow → massive RAAS activation → hypertension resistant to most drugs except ACEi/ARBs (with caution)
secondary_hypertension_causes.clues: Flash pulmonary oedema, renal bruit, worsening renal function on ACEi/ARB, young woman (fibromuscular dysplasia) or elderly atherosclerosis
secondary_hypertension_causes.diagnosis: Renal Doppler ultrasound, CT angiography, MR angiography

secondary_hypertension_causes.mechanism: Autonomous aldosterone secretion causes sodium retention, potassium wasting, and volume-dependent hypertension
secondary_hypertension_causes.clues: Hypokalemia (spontaneous or with diuretics), resistant hypertension, adrenal adenoma or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia on imaging
secondary_hypertension_causes.diagnosis: Aldosterone-to-Renin Ratio (ARR) >30 (screening); adrenal CT; adrenal vein sampling
secondary_hypertension_causes.prevalence: 5-10% of hypertension (most common secondary endocrine cause)

secondary_hypertension_causes.mechanism: Paroxysmal catecholamine (adrenaline/noradrenaline) release from adrenal medulla tumour → severe episodic hypertension
secondary_hypertension_causes.clues: Paroxysmal headache-palpitations-sweating triad, pallor, hypertensive crises, weight loss
secondary_hypertension_causes.diagnosis: 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines; plasma metanephrines; adrenal CT/MRI
secondary_hypertension_causes.prevalence: <1%; the '5% tumour' — 5% malignant, 5% bilateral, 5% extra-adrenal, 5% hereditary, 5% in children

secondary_hypertension_causes.mechanism: Repeated hypoxia during sleep → sympathetic activation → nocturnal and sustained daytime hypertension; non-dipping nocturnal BP pattern
secondary_hypertension_causes.clues: Obesity (BMI>30), loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas, daytime somnolence (Epworth Score >10), collar size >17 inches men, morning headaches
secondary_hypertension_causes.diagnosis: Overnight polysomnography (sleep study); ApneaLink home oximetry screening
secondary_hypertension_causes.prevalence: Very common; present in >30% of hypertension; up to 85% of resistant hypertension

secondary_hypertension_causes.mechanism: Cortisol excess → glucocorticoid-mediated sodium retention, increased angiotensinogen, weight gain
secondary_hypertension_causes.clues: Central obesity (moon face, buffalo hump), purple/red striae, proximal myopathy, easy bruising, hyperglycemia, osteoporosis
secondary_hypertension_causes.diagnosis: 24-hour urine free cortisol, overnight 1mg dexamethasone suppression test, late-night salivary cortisol

secondary_hypertension_causes.mechanism: Various mechanisms including sodium retention, sympathomimetic effects, RAAS stimulation
drugs: NSAIDs and COX-2 inhibitors — sodium retention; blunt antihypertensive efficacy
Oral Contraceptive Pills (OCP) — oestrogen-mediated RAAS activation (dose-dependent)
Calcineurin inhibitors (ciclosporin, tacrolimus) — vasoconstriction, sodium retention
Erythropoietin — increased red cell mass and vasoconstriction

secondary_hypertension_causes.mechanism: Hyperthyroidism: increased cardiac output, tachycardia, wide pulse pressure, systolic HTN. Hypothyroidism: increased peripheral resistance, diastolic HTN
Congenital narrowing of the aorta causing hypertension proximal to the narrowing (arms) and hypotension distal (legs)
secondary_hypertension_causes.clues: Young patient; arm BP much higher than leg BP; radio-femoral pulse delay; rib notching on CXR; ejection systolic murmur

symptoms.important_note: Hypertension is known as the 'SILENT KILLER' — the vast majority of patients (over 80%) have NO symptoms, even with significantly elevated blood pressure. This is precisely why hypertension is so dangerous — it causes progressive target organ damage without warning. Regular blood pressure screening is the only way to detect it.

primary_symptoms.name: Headache — Occipital, Early Morning
primary_symptoms.description: Hypertensive headache classically occurs in the occipital (back of head) region, typically on waking in the morning, and may improve as the day progresses. More common with severe or poorly controlled hypertension. However, headache is NOT a reliable symptom of routine hypertension — many patients with very high BP have no headache, and most headaches are NOT caused by hypertension.
primary_symptoms.onset: Typically on waking in morning; occipital and throbbing
primary_symptoms.note: Severe sudden 'thunderclap' headache (worst headache of life) requires IMMEDIATE emergency evaluation — possible subarachnoid haemorrhage or hypertensive encephalopathy

primary_symptoms.name: Dizziness and Lightheadedness
primary_symptoms.description: Intermittent dizziness may occur, particularly with severe hypertension or when BP fluctuates. Can also result from over-treatment causing hypotension, especially in elderly. Dizziness alone is a poor predictor of hypertension.
primary_symptoms.onset: Episodic; may worsen on standing (if orthostatic hypotension from medication)

primary_symptoms.name: Epistaxis (Nosebleeds)
primary_symptoms.description: Recurrent or severe nosebleeds are associated with hypertension, particularly when BP is very high. Hypertension does not directly cause epistaxis but elevated BP can worsen bleeding from minor mucosal trauma. Severe spontaneous epistaxis with very high BP warrants BP measurement.

primary_symptoms.name: Visual Disturbances
primary_symptoms.description: Blurred vision, double vision, or sudden visual loss can result from hypertensive retinopathy (damage to retinal blood vessels from chronic high BP) or from acute hypertensive emergencies causing papilloedema, retinal haemorrhage, or central retinal artery/vein occlusion. Sudden vision loss in a hypertensive patient is an emergency.
primary_symptoms.severity: Mild (chronic retinopathy) to Severe (acute hypertensive emergency with vision loss)

primary_symptoms.name: Palpitations and Tachycardia
primary_symptoms.description: Awareness of heartbeat, racing heart, or irregular heart rhythm. Hypertension promotes left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), atrial enlargement, and atrial fibrillation. Palpitations in a hypertensive patient warrant ECG and Holter monitoring.

primary_symptoms.name: Fatigue and Reduced Exercise Tolerance
primary_symptoms.description: Non-specific but common in hypertension. Results from cardiac remodelling (LVH, diastolic dysfunction), anaemia of renal disease in hypertensive nephropathy, or medication side effects. Fatigue combined with breathlessness on exertion suggests possible hypertensive heart disease.

secondary_symptoms: Chest pain or pressure (angina) — hypertension accelerates coronary atherosclerosis and increases myocardial oxygen demand
Shortness of breath — hypertensive heart failure (diastolic dysfunction), pulmonary oedema in hypertensive emergency
Facial flushing — episodic; from sympathetic activation or pheochromocytoma
Sweating (diaphoresis) — profuse sweating with severe hypertension or pheochromocytoma
Tinnitus (ringing in ears) — associated with high BP but not specific
Neck pain and stiffness — associated with very high BP; meningism in subarachnoid haemorrhage
Confusion or cognitive difficulty — chronic hypertension damages cerebral small vessels causing white matter lesions and vascular dementia
Haematuria (blood in urine) — hypertensive nephropathy; glomerulosclerosis
Nocturia (frequent urination at night) — common in hypertensive kidney disease from impaired urinary concentration
Cold extremities — peripheral artery disease from atherosclerosis accelerated by hypertension
Erectile dysfunction and reduced libido — vascular insufficiency from hypertension and atherosclerosis; also common antihypertensive drug side effect
warning_signs_of_attack: Sudden severe 'thunderclap' headache — worst headache of life — possible subarachnoid haemorrhage or hypertensive emergency
Sudden weakness or paralysis of face, arm, or leg (especially one-sided) — possible stroke from hypertension
Sudden slurred speech, aphasia, or facial drooping — stroke (FAST mnemonic: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services)
Sudden loss of vision in one or both eyes — hypertensive emergency, retinal artery occlusion, or stroke
Severe chest pain radiating to back — possible aortic dissection (surgical emergency); characteristic tearing pain; BP differential between arms
Acute breathlessness at rest — possible hypertensive pulmonary oedema; acute heart failure
Confusion, altered consciousness, agitation — hypertensive encephalopathy; intracranial haemorrhage
symptoms_in_children: Often completely asymptomatic — detected incidentally during school health screening
Headache — particularly occipital or frontal; often dismissed as tension headache
Blurred vision or visual changes — hypertensive retinopathy
Bell's palsy (facial nerve palsy) — associated with severe hypertension in children
Failure to thrive in infants with severe secondary hypertension
Secondary cause far more common in children than adults — renal disease (most common), coarctation of aorta, endocrine causes must be investigated

medical_history: Duration and severity of hypertension; previous BP readings and treatment history
Cardiovascular risk factors: smoking status, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia, family history of premature CVD
Symptoms of target organ damage: chest pain, dyspnoea, palpitations, headache, visual changes, focal neurological symptoms, haematuria, oedema

Symptoms suggesting secondary hypertension: sweating/palpitation episodes (phaeochromocytoma); muscle weakness/cramps with diuretics (primary aldosteronism); symptoms of sleep apnoea; symptoms of thyroid disease; symptoms of Cushing's
Current and past medications — including OCP, NSAIDs, steroids, decongestants, herbal remedies
Dietary history: sodium intake (processed foods, added salt), alcohol consumption, caffeine intake
Previous cardiovascular events: MI, stroke, TIA, heart failure, peripheral artery disease, renal disease
Family history: hypertension, premature cardiovascular disease, stroke, kidney disease, diabetes
physical_examination: BP measurement: properly seated patient, after 5 minutes rest; correct cuff size (bladder 80% of arm circumference); average of ≥2 readings; both arms on first visit (higher reading is the reference arm)
Standing BP measurement: to detect orthostatic hypotension (fall >20 mmHg SBP or >10 mmHg DBP on standing) — especially important in elderly and those on antihypertensives
Heart rate measurement — bradycardia (beta-blockers), tachycardia (anxiety, phaeochromocytoma, anaemia)
Weight and height — BMI calculation (obesity is a major modifiable risk factor)
Waist circumference — abdominal obesity (>102cm men; >88cm women) increases metabolic and cardiovascular risk
Cardiovascular examination: apex beat (displaced in LVH or cardiomegaly); S4 heart sound (LVH/non-compliant ventricle); murmurs; peripheral pulses; bilateral ankle oedema
Peripheral pulses and BP in both legs (compare with arms for coarctation)
Auscultation for bruits: carotid bruit (cerebrovascular disease); renal artery bruit at epigastrium/flanks (renovascular hypertension)
Fundoscopy: hypertensive retinopathy classification (Keith-Wagener-Barker grades I-IV); papilloedema (grade IV = hypertensive emergency)
Neurological examination: for focal deficits indicating previous or current stroke/TIA
Abdominal examination: enlarged kidneys (polycystic kidneys); renal bruit; adrenal mass
Signs of secondary causes: moon face, buffalo hump, striae (Cushing's); goitre (thyroid); cushingoid features

blood_pressure_measurement_methods.office_measurement: Standard clinical measurement; at least 2 readings 1-2 minutes apart on 2 separate visits; average used; reference standard for diagnosis

abpm_ambulatory.description: Gold standard — 24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring; automatic cuff measures BP every 15-30 minutes over 24 hours during normal activities and sleep
abpm_ambulatory.advantages: Detects white coat HTN, masked HTN, nocturnal dipping pattern, morning surge; best predictor of cardiovascular outcomes
abpm_ambulatory.thresholds: ABPM: Daytime average ≥135/85 = hypertension; 24h average ≥130/80 = hypertension; Nighttime average ≥120/70 = hypertension
abpm_ambulatory.dipping: Normal: >10% fall in nocturnal BP (dipper); Non-dipper or reverse dipper patterns associated with worse cardiovascular outcomes

home_bp_monitoring.description: Self-measurement at home with validated device; 2 readings morning and evening for 7 days; discard day 1 readings
home_bp_monitoring.advantages: Identifies white coat and masked HTN; improves adherence; inexpensive

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Full Blood Count (FBC) / Complete Blood Count (CBC)
diagnostic_tests.description: Screens for anaemia (can cause secondary hypertension or exacerbate cardiac workload); polycythaemia (increases blood viscosity and BP); thrombocytopenia in pre-eclampsia (HELLP syndrome).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Baseline assessment; detect anaemia, polycythaemia; screen for HELLP in pregnancy
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Hb <120 g/L (women) or <130 g/L (men) = anaemia; Hb >185 (men) or >165 (women) = polycythaemia

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Renal Function Tests (Serum Creatinine, eGFR, Urea)
diagnostic_tests.description: Essential baseline test — both to detect pre-existing CKD causing hypertension AND to assess kidney function before prescribing RAAS-blocking antihypertensives (ACEi/ARBs). Creatinine rise >20% after starting ACEi/ARB suggests renovascular disease.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect CKD; baseline before antihypertensive therapy; dose adjustment of medications; detect hypertensive nephropathy progression
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73m² = CKD; Creatinine >120 µmol/L (men) or >110 µmol/L (women) = impaired renal function

diagnostic_tests.description: Hypokalaemia (low potassium) is a key clue for primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome) and Cushing's syndrome. Hypernatraemia with hypertension suggests excess mineralocorticoid activity. Bicarbonate elevated in metabolic alkalosis (hyperaldosteronism).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for secondary hypertension; baseline before diuretic therapy; monitor during treatment
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Hypokalaemia (<3.5 mmol/L spontaneously or with standard diuretic doses) — screen for primary aldosteronism; hypernatraemia + hypertension → secondary cause

diagnostic_tests.description: Diabetes and hypertension frequently coexist (~50% of type 2 diabetics are hypertensive) and synergistically increase cardiovascular risk. HbA1c provides 3-month average glucose control. Essential for overall cardiovascular risk stratification.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose diabetes/pre-diabetes; cardiovascular risk assessment; guides BP target (stricter <130/80 in diabetes)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Fasting glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) = diabetes; 6.1-6.9 mmol/L (110-125 mg/dL) = impaired fasting glucose; HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol (6.5%) = diabetes

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Fasting Lipid Profile (Total Cholesterol, LDL, HDL, Triglycerides)
diagnostic_tests.description: Dyslipidaemia is a major cardiovascular risk factor that coexists with hypertension in 30-40% of patients. Total cardiovascular risk assessment requires lipid profile. Most hypertensive patients with additional risk factors require statin therapy regardless of cholesterol level.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Cardiovascular risk stratification (SCORE2 / Framingham risk score / QRisk3); guide statin therapy decision
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: LDL >4.9 mmol/L (190 mg/dL): very high CV risk; LDL target varies by overall CV risk category

diagnostic_tests.description: Urine dipstick screens for proteinuria, haematuria, and glucose. Urine ACR (or PCR) detects microalbuminuria — the earliest marker of hypertensive nephropathy. Microalbuminuria is an independent cardiovascular risk marker. Mandatory in all hypertensive patients at diagnosis and annually.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect hypertensive nephropathy (microalbuminuria); screen for diabetic nephropathy; detect haematuria (renal disease); diagnose proteinuria (pre-eclampsia in pregnancy)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Microalbuminuria: ACR 3-30 mg/mmol (30-300 mg/g); Macroalbuminuria (proteinuria): ACR >30 mg/mmol; Haematuria: ≥3 RBCs/hpf

diagnostic_tests.description: Detects Left Ventricular Hypertrophy (LVH) — the most important cardiac consequence of hypertension. LVH on ECG (Sokolow-Lyon index: SV1+RV5 >35mm; Cornell product; Romhild index) is associated with 3-fold increased risk of cardiac events. Also detects arrhythmias (AF — major hypertension complication), ST/T changes (ischaemia), and left bundle branch block.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect LVH (most important target organ damage marker); atrial fibrillation; ischaemic changes; arrhythmias
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Sokolow-Lyon: SV1+RV5 ≥35mm = LVH; PR interval prolongation; P-wave changes (LAH); AF on rhythm strip

diagnostic_tests.description: Most sensitive and specific test for LVH (more sensitive than ECG). Also assesses left ventricular function (systolic and diastolic), aortic root size, valvular disease, and pericardium. Diastolic dysfunction (impaired LV relaxation) is an early hypertensive cardiac consequence.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect LVH (gold standard), diastolic dysfunction, systolic function assessment, aortic root assessment, valvular disease
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: LV mass index >115 g/m² (men) or >95 g/m² (women) = LVH; LAVI >34 mL/m² = LA enlargement; E/e' ratio >14 = diastolic dysfunction

diagnostic_tests.description: Both hyperthyroidism (systolic hypertension, wide pulse pressure) and hypothyroidism (diastolic hypertension) can cause or worsen hypertension. TSH is the best single screening test.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for thyroid disease as a secondary cause of hypertension; routine in all newly diagnosed patients
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: TSH <0.4 mIU/L (hyperthyroidism); TSH >4.0 mIU/L (hypothyroidism); Free T4 for confirmation

diagnostic_tests.description: First-line screening test for primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome) — the most common secondary endocrine cause of hypertension. Elevated aldosterone with suppressed renin (high ARR) is characteristic. Must stop spironolactone, eplerenone, and ARBs before testing.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for primary hyperaldosteronism in resistant hypertension, hypokalaemic hypertension, and patients <40 with Grade 2+ hypertension
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: ARR >30 (ng/dL)/(ng/mL/hr) with aldosterone >15 ng/dL is a positive screening result; confirm with salt loading test or fludrocortisone suppression test

diagnostic_tests.description: 24-hour urine fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines (or plasma free metanephrines) are the best tests for pheochromocytoma. Plasma free metanephrines have highest sensitivity (~99%).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for pheochromocytoma in: paroxysmal hypertension, hypertensive crises, incidentally discovered adrenal mass, family history of phaeochromocytoma/MEN2
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Plasma metanephrines >3x upper limit of normal is highly specific for phaeochromocytoma; mildly elevated values common with anxiety, medications — confirmatory testing required

diagnostic_tests.description: First-line imaging for renal parenchymal disease (polycystic kidneys, asymmetric kidneys), renovascular disease (renal artery Doppler), and adrenal masses. Renal Doppler assesses renal artery stenosis (peak systolic velocity >200 cm/s, resistive index).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect renal parenchymal disease, renal artery stenosis (renovascular HTN), adrenal masses
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Asymmetry in kidney size >1.5 cm suggests renovascular disease; renal artery PSV >200 cm/s suggests stenosis

diagnostic_tests.description: Examination of retinal blood vessels directly mirrors the state of small vessels throughout the body. Keith-Wagener-Barker (KWB) grading system: Grade I (arterial narrowing, copper wiring); Grade II (AV nipping); Grade III (flame haemorrhages, cotton wool spots — hypertensive urgency/emergency); Grade IV (papilloedema — hypertensive emergency). Grade III-IV = hypertensive emergency.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess target organ damage in retinal vessels; detect hypertensive emergency (papilloedema); grade severity of hypertensive retinopathy
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: KWB Grade III-IV (haemorrhages, exudates, papilloedema) = hypertensive emergency requiring immediate treatment

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Carotid Intima-Media Thickness (CIMT) and Carotid Ultrasound
diagnostic_tests.description: Measures the thickness of the inner two layers of the carotid artery wall — a surrogate marker of subclinical atherosclerosis. Elevated CIMT is an independent cardiovascular risk marker. Also detects carotid plaques.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess subclinical atherosclerosis; risk stratification; detect carotid plaques
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: CIMT >0.9mm = increased subclinical atherosclerosis; plaques = established atherosclerosis (high CV risk)

medicines.note: All antihypertensive medications must be prescribed, initiated, and monitored by a licensed physician or cardiologist. Self-adjustment or discontinuation of antihypertensive therapy is dangerous and can precipitate hypertensive crisis. Treatment should be individualized based on age, ethnicity, comorbidities, BP level, and side effect profile.
treatment_principles: BP target: <140/90 mmHg for most adults; <130/80 mmHg for high-risk patients (diabetes, CKD, established CVD, prior stroke — per ACC/AHA)
Single drug therapy (monotherapy) for Grade 1 hypertension in low-moderate CV risk
Combination therapy from outset for Grade 2-3 hypertension, or Grade 1 with high CV risk
Preferred combinations: ACEi or ARB + CCB; ACEi or ARB + thiazide diuretic; CCB + thiazide diuretic
ACEi and ARBs must NEVER be combined (increased risk of hyperkalaemia, AKI, hypotension — ALTITUDE and ONTARGET trials)
Renin system blockade (ACEi or ARB) preferred in: diabetes, CKD, proteinuria, post-MI, systolic heart failure
CCBs and thiazide diuretics preferred first-line in: Black/African American patients, elderly isolated systolic HTN
Treat-to-target approach: reassess BP response every 4-8 weeks; step up therapy if target not achieved

categories.purpose: Block conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II (the RAAS), reducing vasoconstriction, aldosterone secretion, sodium retention, and cardiac and renal fibrosis. First-line for hypertension, especially with diabetes, CKD, proteinuria, heart failure, or post-MI.
categories.onset: BP reduction within hours; full effect in 4-6 weeks

medicines.name: Ramipril
medicines.dosage: Starting: 2.5 mg once daily; maintenance: 5-10 mg once daily; heart failure: titrate to 10 mg/day
medicines.use_case: Hypertension; heart failure with reduced EF (HFrEF); post-MI with LV dysfunction; diabetic nephropathy; stroke prevention (HOPE trial benefit)
medicines.mechanism: Inhibits ACE; reduces angiotensin II and aldosterone; reduces afterload, preload, and cardiac remodelling
side_effects: Dry, persistent cough (10-20% — class effect; most common reason for switching to ARB)
Acute Kidney Injury — renal function worsens by >20%: stop drug (bilateral renal artery stenosis contraindication)
Angioedema (rare but life-threatening — swelling of face, lips, tongue, throat — STOP immediately; class contraindication to future ACEi use)
contraindications: Combination with aliskiren in diabetes or CKD
medicines.monitoring: Serum creatinine, eGFR, and potassium at 1-4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase; annually thereafter

medicines.name: Lisinopril
medicines.dosage: Starting: 2.5-5 mg once daily; maintenance: 10-40 mg once daily
medicines.use_case: Hypertension; heart failure; post-MI; diabetic nephropathy

medicines.name: Enalapril
medicines.dosage: Starting: 2.5-5 mg twice daily; maintenance: 10-20 mg twice daily
medicines.use_case: Hypertension; heart failure (CONSENSUS and SOLVD landmark trials established ACEi in heart failure)

medicines.name: Perindopril
medicines.dosage: 4-8 mg once daily (arginine salt: 5-10 mg); starting 2-4 mg
medicines.use_case: Hypertension; stable coronary artery disease (EUROPA trial benefit); stroke prevention (combined with indapamide in PROGRESS trial)

categories.purpose: Block angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) receptor — the effector receptor for vasoconstriction and aldosterone release. Equally effective as ACEi but WITHOUT the dry cough (key advantage). Preferred in patients who develop ACEi cough. First-line for hypertension, CKD, diabetes, heart failure (ACEi-intolerant).

medicines.name: Losartan
medicines.dosage: Starting: 25-50 mg once daily; maintenance: 50-100 mg once daily
medicines.use_case: Hypertension; diabetic nephropathy in type 2 DM (RENAAL trial); LVH reduction (LIFE trial — superior to atenolol for stroke prevention); gout (mild uricosuric effect — useful if gout comorbidity)
medicines.mechanism: Selective AT1 receptor antagonist; blocks angiotensin II effects; no effect on bradykinin (no cough)
side_effects: Angioedema (significantly rarer than ACEi but possible)
medicines.unique_benefit: Mild uricosuric effect reduces uric acid levels — useful in hypertensive patients with gout or hyperuricemia

medicines.name: Telmisartan
medicines.dosage: Starting: 20-40 mg once daily; maintenance: 40-80 mg once daily
medicines.use_case: Hypertension; cardiovascular protection in high-risk patients (ONTARGET — non-inferior to ramipril); longest half-life of all ARBs (24h) — ideal once-daily drug for adherence
medicines.unique_benefit: Longest half-life (24 hours) → best 24-hour BP coverage; mild PPAR-gamma agonism may improve insulin sensitivity

medicines.name: Valsartan
medicines.dosage: 80-160 mg once daily; maximum 320 mg/day
medicines.use_case: Hypertension; heart failure (Val-HeFT); post-MI LV dysfunction (VALIANT — equivalent to captopril)

medicines.name: Olmesartan
medicines.dosage: 10-20 mg once daily; maximum 40 mg/day
medicines.use_case: Hypertension; one of the most potent ARBs in BP-lowering; atherosclerosis prevention (OLIVUS trial)
medicines.note: Associated with sprue-like enteropathy (severe diarrhoea, weight loss) with prolonged use — rare but important to recognize

medicines.name: Candesartan
medicines.dosage: 4-8 mg once daily; maximum 32 mg/day
medicines.use_case: Hypertension; heart failure (CHARM trials — reduced mortality); migraine prevention (off-label)

categories.purpose: Block voltage-gated L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle and cardiac cells, causing vasodilation and reduced vascular resistance. Dihydropyridines act predominantly on peripheral vasculature; non-dihydropyridines also slow heart rate and AV conduction.

medicines.name: Amlodipine
medicines.dosage: Starting: 2.5-5 mg once daily; maintenance: 5-10 mg once daily
medicines.use_case: MOST WIDELY USED antihypertensive globally; hypertension (first-line); stable and vasospastic angina; isolated systolic hypertension in elderly; Black/African American patients; ALLHAT trial — superior CV outcomes vs ACEi in some groups
medicines.mechanism: Dihydropyridine CCB; predominantly peripheral vasodilation; long half-life (35-50 hours) → smooth 24-hour BP control; minimal heart rate effect
side_effects: Peripheral oedema — ankle swelling (most common; dose-dependent; from arteriolar vasodilation with preserved venous tone; not fluid retention)
Palpitations and reflex tachycardia (minimal with amlodipine vs shorter-acting CCBs)
Gingival hyperplasia (overgrowth of gum tissue — with prolonged use)
medicines.note: Ankle oedema can be reduced by: adding ACEi/ARB (co-prescription reduces oedema by ~50%); combining with diuretic; raising legs; switching to different CCB

medicines.name: Nifedipine (Modified Release / Extended Release)
medicines.dosage: 30-60 mg once daily (SR/LA/GITS formulation); 20-40 mg twice daily (retard)
medicines.use_case: Hypertension; Raynaud's phenomenon; angina; preterm labour (tocolysis off-label); ONLY use modified-release formulations for hypertension
medicines.warning: SHORT-ACTING sublingual nifedipine (immediate-release capsule) is ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED for hypertensive emergencies — causes unpredictable, rapid BP drops, reflex tachycardia, and has caused fatal MI and stroke

medicines.name: Felodipine
medicines.dosage: 2.5-10 mg once daily
medicines.use_case: Hypertension; heart failure (unlike most CCBs, felodipine and amlodipine are safe in heart failure — Vdal-HeFT)
medicines.note: Grapefruit juice significantly increases felodipine plasma levels (CYP3A4 inhibition) — counsel patients to avoid grapefruit

medicines.name: Diltiazem (Non-Dihydropyridine CCB)
medicines.dosage: Hypertension: 120-240 mg SR once or twice daily; Angina: 60-120 mg three times daily standard-release
medicines.use_case: Hypertension with tachyarrhythmia or supraventricular tachycardia; angina; rate control in atrial flutter/fibrillation; NOT suitable with heart failure with reduced EF (negative inotropic effect)
medicines.mechanism: Non-dihydropyridine CCB; acts on both peripheral vessels AND cardiac cells (negative chronotropy, negative dromotropy); reduces heart rate and AV conduction
contraindications: Combination with verapamil or beta-blockers (additive heart block risk)

medicines.name: Verapamil (Non-Dihydropyridine CCB)
medicines.dosage: Hypertension: 240-360 mg SR once daily
medicines.use_case: Hypertension; SVT; rate control AF; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; migraine prevention
contraindications: Combination with beta-blockers (serious AV block risk)

categories.purpose: Initially reduce blood pressure by promoting sodium and water excretion (volume depletion). Long-term BP reduction from direct arterial vasodilation through reduced vascular reactivity. Particularly effective in elderly, isolated systolic hypertension, and Black/African American patients.

medicines.name: Indapamide
medicines.dosage: 1.5 mg SR once daily (preferred); 2.5 mg standard
medicines.use_case: PREFERRED thiazide-like diuretic — lower metabolic side effects than hydrochlorothiazide; reduces LVH; reduces stroke (PROGRESS trial with perindopril); CKD preferred over HCTZ (remains effective at lower GFR)
side_effects: Hyponatraemia (low sodium — especially in elderly women)
Hypokalemia (potassium loss — consider K-sparing agent or monitor)
medicines.monitoring: Electrolytes (Na+, K+), renal function, uric acid at 4-8 weeks; annually thereafter

medicines.name: Chlorthalidone
medicines.dosage: 12.5-25 mg once daily
medicines.use_case: Preferred thiazide-like in USA (ALLHAT used chlorthalidone); longer duration of action than HCTZ; better 24-hour BP coverage; more effective in reducing cardiovascular events

medicines.name: Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ)
medicines.dosage: 12.5-25 mg once daily; maximum 50 mg/day
medicines.use_case: Hypertension; oedema; combination formulations with ACEi or ARB (e.g., perindopril/indapamide, losartan/HCTZ); frequently used as part of fixed-dose combinations
medicines.note: Less effective at lower eGFR (<30); chlorthalidone or indapamide preferred over HCTZ in most situations when specifically choosing a thiazide-like diuretic

categories.purpose: Reduce heart rate and cardiac output; block sympathetic stimulation of the heart; reduce renin release. Not recommended as first-line for uncomplicated hypertension (less effective than other first-line agents for stroke prevention) but essential first-line in specific situations.
categories.specific_indications: Post-MI, stable angina, heart failure with reduced EF (HFrEF), atrial fibrillation (rate control), hypertension in pregnancy (labetalol), phaeochromocytoma (after alpha-blocker), young patients with sympathetic hyperactivity

medicines.name: Bisoprolol
medicines.dosage: Starting 2.5-5 mg once daily; maximum 10-20 mg/day
medicines.use_case: Hypertension (2nd-line); FIRST-LINE in: HFrEF (CIBIS-II trial); stable angina; post-MI; atrial fibrillation rate control
medicines.mechanism: Highly cardioselective beta-1 blocker; minimal beta-2 blockade — safer in mild asthma/COPD than non-selective
side_effects: Masking hypoglycaemia symptoms (in diabetes — blunts tachycardia; sweating preserved)
contraindications: Sick sinus syndrome or 2nd/3rd degree AV block without pacemaker

medicines.name: Atenolol
medicines.dosage: 25-50 mg once daily; maximum 100 mg/day
medicines.use_case: Hypertension; angina; post-MI; commonly used but LIFE trial showed losartan superior for stroke prevention
medicines.note: Renal excretion — dose reduce in CKD

medicines.name: Metoprolol Succinate (Extended Release)
medicines.dosage: Starting 25-50 mg once daily; maximum 200 mg/day
medicines.use_case: HFrEF (MERIT-HF trial — reduced mortality); hypertension; post-MI; angina; AF rate control
side_effects: Worsening heart failure if titrated too fast

medicines.name: Carvedilol
medicines.dosage: Starting: 3.125-6.25 mg twice daily; target: 25 mg twice daily (titrate over weeks)
medicines.use_case: HFrEF (COPERNICUS, CAPRICORN trials); hypertension; vasodilatory properties from alpha-1 blockade in addition to non-selective beta blockade
medicines.mechanism: Non-selective beta-blocker + alpha-1 blocker; vasodilatory; anti-oxidant properties
side_effects: Dizziness (from alpha blockade causing orthostatic hypotension)
Worsening heart failure if started at high dose

medicines.name: Labetalol
medicines.dosage: Oral: 100-400 mg twice daily; IV: 20-80 mg boluses or 2 mg/min infusion
medicines.use_case: PREFERRED in pregnancy hypertension (safe in all trimesters); hypertensive emergencies (IV); phaeochromocytoma (after alpha-blockers established)
medicines.mechanism: Non-selective beta-blocker + alpha-1 blocker; combined mechanisms lower both cardiac output and peripheral resistance

medicines.name: Nebivolol
medicines.dosage: 2.5-5 mg once daily; maximum 10 mg/day
medicines.use_case: Hypertension; HFrEF; unique advantage: releases nitric oxide causing vasodilation — significantly less erectile dysfunction than other beta-blockers
medicines.mechanism: Highly selective beta-1 blocker + endothelium-dependent vasodilation via nitric oxide release
side_effects: Lowest rate of erectile dysfunction among beta-blockers

categories.purpose: Block aldosterone receptors preventing sodium retention and potassium loss. Most effective 4th-line drug for resistant hypertension. Essential in heart failure with reduced EF.

medicines.name: Spironolactone
medicines.dosage: Resistant HTN: 25-50 mg once daily; HF: start 12.5-25 mg; maximum 50-100 mg/day
medicines.use_case: MOST EFFECTIVE 4th-line drug for resistant hypertension (PATHWAY-2 trial — superior to bisoprolol and doxazosin); primary hyperaldosteronism; HFrEF (RALES trial); ascites in cirrhosis
side_effects: Hyperkalaemia (monitor closely — DANGEROUS if added to ACEi/ARB; avoid if K+ >5.0 mmol/L)
Gynaecomastia and breast tenderness in men (common, dose-dependent)
medicines.monitoring: Renal function and potassium at 1 week and 4 weeks after starting; monthly for first 3 months; contraindicated with eGFR <30 or K+ >5.0
medicines.note: Gynaecomastia can be switched to eplerenone (more selective, less antiandrogenic)

medicines.name: Eplerenone
medicines.dosage: 25-50 mg once daily
medicines.use_case: Resistant hypertension; post-MI HFrEF (EPHESUS trial); alternative to spironolactone without gynaecomastia
side_effects: No gynaecomastia (selective MRA — less antiandrogenic effects)
medicines.monitoring: Renal function and potassium; more expensive than spironolactone

categories.purpose: Most potent diuretics — block Na-K-2Cl transporter in thick ascending limb of loop of Henle. Not first-line for hypertension in normal renal function but essential when hypertension is complicated by CKD (where thiazides lose efficacy at eGFR <30), heart failure, or volume overload states.

medicines.name: Furosemide (Frusemide)
medicines.dosage: Hypertension + CKD: 40-80 mg once or twice daily; Heart failure oedema: 20-240 mg/day titrated; IV for acute pulmonary oedema: 40-80 mg IV
medicines.use_case: Hypertension + CKD (eGFR <30); hypertensive emergency with pulmonary oedema; heart failure; nephrotic syndrome; resistant HTN with volume overload
side_effects: Hypokalaemia (supplement potassium or add K-sparing agent)
medicines.monitoring: Electrolytes (Na+, K+, Mg2+) and renal function regularly

medicines.name: Torasemide (Torsemide)
medicines.dosage: 5-20 mg once daily
medicines.use_case: Hypertension + CKD; heart failure (better bioavailability than furosemide; no post-diuretic sodium retention; may have anti-fibrotic effects)

categories.purpose: Block alpha-1 receptors in peripheral arterioles, causing vasodilation and BP reduction. Not recommended as first-line antihypertensives (ALLHAT showed higher heart failure risk than thiazides) but useful as add-on therapy in resistant hypertension and specifically for hypertension with benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).

medicines.name: Doxazosin
medicines.dosage: Starting: 1 mg once daily at bedtime (first dose effect); maintenance: 2-8 mg once daily (MR); maximum 16 mg/day
medicines.use_case: Resistant hypertension (3rd or 4th agent); hypertension + BPH (dual indication — relaxes prostate smooth muscle and reduces BP); pheochromocytoma (pre-operative alpha blockade)
medicines.mechanism: Selective alpha-1 blocker; peripheral vasodilation; also relaxes bladder neck and prostate smooth muscle
side_effects: First-dose postural hypotension (start at night — take at bedtime)
medicines.note: Always start at lowest dose at bedtime to prevent first-dose syncope

medicines.name: Prazosin
medicines.dosage: 0.5-1 mg twice or three times daily; maximum 20 mg/day
medicines.use_case: Resistant hypertension; BPH; Raynaud's phenomenon; PTSD (off-label: reduces nightmares)

categories.purpose: Act on alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem, reducing sympathetic outflow to heart and blood vessels. Methyldopa is the drug of choice in pregnancy.

medicines.name: Methyldopa
medicines.dosage: 250 mg two to three times daily; maximum 3 g/day (pregnancy: 250 mg three times daily, maximum 3g/day)
medicines.use_case: DRUG OF CHOICE for hypertension in pregnancy (all trimesters; extensive safety data; used for >50 years in pregnancy); refractory hypertension add-on
medicines.mechanism: Centrally-acting alpha-2 agonist; reduces sympathetic outflow from CNS; decreases heart rate, cardiac output, and peripheral resistance

medicines.name: Clonidine
medicines.dosage: 0.1-0.3 mg twice or three times daily; transdermal patch weekly
medicines.use_case: Resistant or refractory hypertension add-on; opiate withdrawal; ADHD (off-label); menopausal flushing
side_effects: Rebound hypertension on abrupt withdrawal (potentially dangerous — do not stop abruptly)
medicines.warning: Rebound hypertensive crisis with abrupt discontinuation — always taper gradually

categories.purpose: Directly relax arteriolar smooth muscle causing vasodilation and BP reduction. Limited first-line use due to reflex tachycardia, sodium retention, and fluid retention side effects — typically used as add-on in resistant or refractory hypertension.

medicines.name: Hydralazine
medicines.dosage: Oral: 25-50 mg two to four times daily; IV for hypertensive emergency in pregnancy: 5-10 mg IV bolus every 20-30 minutes
medicines.use_case: Hypertensive emergencies in pregnancy (IV); severe heart failure as add-on (BiDil — combined with nitrate in self-identified African Americans); chronic refractory hypertension
side_effects: Drug-induced lupus (slow acetylators at high doses — ANA positive; reversible on stopping)

medicines.name: Minoxidil
medicines.dosage: Starting: 2.5-5 mg once or twice daily; maximum 100 mg/day
medicines.use_case: Severe refractory hypertension (typically 5th or 6th line); most potent oral vasodilator available
side_effects: Severe fluid retention (requires combination with high-dose loop diuretic)
Hirsutism (excessive hair growth — hair growth basis of topical minoxidil)

categories.purpose: Dual-acting: blocks AT1 angiotensin receptor (like ARB) AND inhibits neprilysin (increases natriuretic peptides — causing vasodilation and natriuresis). Primarily for heart failure with reduced EF; growing evidence for hypertension management in HF patients.

medicines.name: Sacubitril-Valsartan (Entresto)
medicines.dosage: Starting: 24/26 mg (sacubitril/valsartan) twice daily; target: 97/103 mg twice daily
medicines.use_case: HFrEF (PARADIGM-HF — superior to enalapril in reducing mortality); may control BP in hypertensive HF patients
medicines.mechanism: Sacubitril inhibits neprilysin (prevents breakdown of ANP, BNP, bradykinin) + valsartan blocks AT1 receptor
side_effects: Angioedema (do NOT use within 36 hours of ACEi — washout required)
medicines.note: Must stop ACEi for 36-hour washout period before starting to prevent angioedema risk (bradykinin potentiation)

categories.category_name: IV Medications for Hypertensive Emergencies (ICU/Hospital Only)
categories.purpose: Intravenous agents for immediate controlled blood pressure reduction in hypertensive emergencies. Always in ICU/monitored setting with arterial line monitoring. Rate of BP reduction must be controlled — too rapid reduction causes ischaemia.
categories.note: Target: reduce BP by 10-20% in first hour; 25% maximum over first 24 hours (EXCEPT: aortic dissection — target SBP <120 within 20 min; ischaemic stroke — reduce only if >220/120 or if thrombolysis planned, do not reduce below 185/110)

medicines.name: Labetalol IV
medicines.dosage: 20-80 mg IV bolus every 10 minutes (max 300 mg); or 0.5-2 mg/min infusion
medicines.use_case: Most common first-line IV agent for hypertensive emergency; aortic dissection (as adjunct); hypertension in pregnancy/eclampsia; post-operative hypertension

medicines.name: Nicardipine IV
medicines.dosage: 5 mg/hour IV; titrate by 2.5 mg/hour every 5 minutes; maximum 15 mg/hour
medicines.use_case: Hypertensive emergencies; perioperative hypertension; ischaemic stroke; pre-eclampsia; preferred in neurological emergencies

medicines.name: Sodium Nitroprusside IV
medicines.dosage: 0.25-10 mcg/kg/min IV infusion; start at lowest dose
medicines.use_case: Hypertensive emergencies requiring precise, immediate BP control; aortic dissection; severe pulmonary oedema; most potent and titratable IV agent
medicines.mechanism: Releases nitric oxide causing direct balanced arterial and venous vasodilation
side_effects: Cyanide and thiocyanate toxicity (prolonged use or renal failure)
Intracranial pressure rise (caution in intracerebral haemorrhage)
medicines.monitoring: Requires intra-arterial BP monitoring; ICU only; limit to 24-48 hours; check thiocyanate levels

medicines.name: Hydralazine IV
medicines.dosage: 5-10 mg IV bolus every 20-30 minutes; maximum 20 mg
medicines.use_case: Hypertensive emergency in pregnancy and eclampsia (widely available globally); pre-eclampsia
medicines.note: Less titratable than labetalol or nicardipine; use when those are unavailable

medicines.name: IV Magnesium Sulfate
medicines.dosage: Loading: 4-6g IV over 15-20 minutes; maintenance: 1-2g/hour infusion
medicines.use_case: ECLAMPSIA — seizure prevention and treatment in pre-eclampsia/eclampsia. Primary indication is anticonvulsant (not antihypertensive per se but reduces cerebrovascular complications). WHO essential medicine for eclampsia.
medicines.monitoring: Respiratory rate (must be ≥12/min); deep tendon reflexes (loss precedes respiratory depression); urine output (>25mL/hr); Mg2+ levels; calcium gluconate antidote must be at bedside

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Diet is the cornerstone of hypertension prevention and management. The DASH diet (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) — the most evidence-based dietary intervention for hypertension — reduces SBP by 8-14 mmHg, comparable to one antihypertensive drug. Combined with sodium restriction, weight loss, exercise, and alcohol reduction, lifestyle changes can reduce BP by 20-30 mmHg — equivalent to combination antihypertensive therapy.

dash_diet_principles.description: DASH diet was developed specifically for hypertension. Rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, low-fat dairy, and limited in saturated fat, red meat, and sweets. High in potassium, calcium, magnesium, and fibre — all nutrients that lower BP.
dash_diet_principles.bp_reduction: DASH diet alone reduces SBP by 8-14 mmHg; combined with sodium restriction reduces SBP by 11-20 mmHg

recommended_foods.evidence: Strong — potassium blunts the pressor effect of sodium; promotes renal sodium excretion; relaxes arterial walls. Adequate potassium intake (3,500-4,700 mg/day) reduces SBP by 3-8 mmHg.

items.benefit: Excellent potassium source (422 mg per banana); easily available; reduces BP and protects against stroke
Very high potassium (941 mg per medium sweet potato); fibre; beta-carotene (antioxidant)
Extremely potassium-dense (708 mg per medium avocado); monounsaturated fats reduce BP; magnesium; fibre
items.frequency: Half avocado daily or several times per week

items.benefit: High potassium (839 mg per cup cooked spinach); dietary nitrates in leafy greens convert to nitric oxide (vasodilatory); magnesium; folate
Potassium (292 mg per cup); lycopene — antioxidant reducing vascular oxidative stress; vitamin C; dietary nitrates
Rich in potassium (600mg per cup); natural electrolyte balance; good for BP management in India

items.food: Legumes: Lentils, Kidney beans, Chickpeas, Dal
items.benefit: Potassium (730mg per cup lentils); plant protein; fibre reduces BP and cholesterol; magnesium; low sodium

recommended_foods.evidence: Strong — magnesium relaxes vascular smooth muscle; magnesium deficiency increases BP; supplementation lowers SBP by 3-4 mmHg

items.benefit: High magnesium; potassium; dietary nitrates for NO production; multiple BP-lowering mechanisms

items.food: Nuts and seeds: Almonds, Pumpkin seeds (unsalted), Flaxseeds, Sesame (til)
items.benefit: Magnesium, potassium, and healthy fats; pumpkin seeds — highest magnesium per serving; flaxseeds — lignans and omega-3 reduce BP

items.food: Whole grains: Oats, Brown rice, Quinoa, Whole wheat
items.benefit: Magnesium; fibre (beta-glucan in oats reduces BP and cholesterol); B vitamins; low glycaemic index
Cocoa flavanols increase nitric oxide bioavailability → vasodilation → BP reduction. Meta-analyses show flavanol-rich cocoa reduces SBP by 2-3 mmHg. High magnesium.
items.frequency: 1-2 small squares (10-20g) daily of ≥70% dark chocolate

recommended_foods.evidence: Moderate — calcium involved in vascular smooth muscle contraction regulation; adequate dietary calcium (1000-1200 mg/day) associated with lower BP

items.food: Low-fat dairy: Skimmed milk, Low-fat curd/yogurt, Buttermilk (chaach)
items.benefit: Calcium; potassium; vitamin D (in fortified milk); protein; DASH diet cornerstone. Buttermilk — low fat, cooling, traditional Indian BP-friendly beverage

items.food: Calcium-fortified plant milks (soy, almond, oat milk)
items.benefit: Dairy alternative; calcium; lower saturated fat than full-fat dairy
High calcium; isoflavones may lower BP; plant protein; magnesium

recommended_foods.evidence: Strong — dietary nitrates converted to nitric oxide (NO) by oral bacteria and intestinal bacteria. NO is the most potent endogenous vasodilator. Beetroot juice trials show SBP reduction of 4-8 mmHg.

items.benefit: Highest dietary nitrate content of any food. Clinical trials: 250mL beetroot juice daily reduces SBP by 4-10 mmHg. Also improves exercise tolerance.
items.frequency: 250-500mL beetroot juice daily; or 1-2 cooked beets daily

items.food: Dark leafy greens: Spinach, Rocket (arugula), Swiss chard, Watercress, Methi
items.benefit: Very high dietary nitrates → NO → vasodilation; potassium; magnesium; multiple synergistic BP-lowering mechanisms
items.frequency: Daily — 2 cups raw or 1 cup cooked

items.benefit: Clinical trials show 5-8 mmHg SBP reduction with 150mL daily for 2 weeks; punicalagins and anthocyanins reduce oxidative stress; ACE-inhibitory activity

recommended_foods.evidence: Strong — EPA and DHA omega-3s reduce SBP by 2-4 mmHg; anti-inflammatory; reduce triglycerides; improve endothelial function

items.food: Fatty fish: Salmon, Mackerel, Sardines, Herring, Indian Rohu, Catla
items.benefit: High EPA and DHA omega-3; direct BP lowering; reduces CV events in hypertensive patients; reduces triglycerides
ALA omega-3; lignans reduce BP; fibre; omega-3:omega-6 balance improves vascular function
items.frequency: 1 tablespoon ground flaxseed daily in yogurt, smoothie, or roti

items.benefit: ALA omega-3; arginine (precursor to nitric oxide — vasodilatory); polyphenols; reduces BP and LDL cholesterol

recommended_foods.category: Specific BP-Lowering Foods with Clinical Evidence

items.food: Garlic (Allium sativum) — 1-2 fresh cloves or garlic extract
items.benefit: Allicin inhibits ACE and calcium channels; meta-analyses show garlic supplementation reduces SBP by 5-9 mmHg and DBP by 4-6 mmHg in hypertensive patients; anti-atherosclerotic; reduces platelet aggregation
items.frequency: 1-2 raw cloves daily (crush and rest 10 min before eating); or 600-900 mg aged garlic extract supplement

items.benefit: Anthocyanins in hibiscus act as ACE inhibitors and calcium channel blockers; RCTs show 5-10 mmHg SBP reduction with 2-3 cups daily in pre-hypertension and Stage 1 HTN

Flavonoids (anthocyanins) improve endothelial function; increase NO bioavailability; reduce arterial stiffness; NHANES data links higher anthocyanin intake with lower BP; blueberry study: 40g/day reduced SBP by 5 mmHg in 8 weeks
Curcumin reduces vascular inflammation and oxidative stress; improves endothelial function; reduces arterial stiffness; meta-analysis shows reduction in SBP with curcumin supplementation
items.frequency: 1/2 tsp daily in cooking, warm milk, or supplement (500-1000 mg twice daily with piperine)

items.benefit: EGCG catechins improve NO availability; reduce vascular oxidative stress; meta-analysis shows 2-3 mmHg SBP reduction with regular green tea; also reduces LDL cholesterol
items.frequency: 2-3 cups daily (not black tea which has higher caffeine)

foods_to_avoid.food: High-Sodium Foods — THE MOST IMPORTANT DIETARY CHANGE
foods_to_avoid.reason: Dietary sodium directly causes volume expansion and vascular stiffness. Every 100 mmol/day reduction in sodium reduces SBP by 5-7 mmHg. WHO recommends <2g sodium per day (5g salt). Most people consume 3.5-5g sodium (8-12g salt).
foods_to_avoid.target: Sodium <2.3g/day (5.75g salt); optimal <1.5g/day (3.75g salt) in hypertension
examples: Table salt (added to food at table) — 1 teaspoon = 2.3g sodium (full daily limit)
Processed meats — sausages, salami, bacon, ham, canned meat — extremely high sodium
Pickles (achaar), papad, chutney powders, salty snacks — very high sodium in Indian diet
Canned and packaged foods — canned soups, ready meals, sauces — hidden sodium
Soy sauce, fish sauce, oyster sauce — 1 tablespoon may contain 900-1,000 mg sodium
Fast food and restaurant meals — single meal may contain full daily sodium allowance
Instant noodles, packaged ramen, instant soups
Bread and baked products — often a surprising hidden sodium source
practical_tips: Cook without adding salt; use herbs, spices (cumin, coriander, turmeric, pepper) and lemon juice for flavor
Read food labels — choose products with <120 mg sodium per 100g
Rinse canned vegetables and legumes to reduce sodium by 40%
Replace salt with potassium chloride salt substitutes (LoSalt) — reduces BP while maintaining flavor
Avoid adding salt at the table

foods_to_avoid.reason: Alcohol raises BP through sympathetic nervous system activation, cortisol release, increased aldosterone, and endothelial dysfunction. Consumption of >3 drinks per day raises SBP by 3-5 mmHg. Heavy drinking is a significant secondary cause of hypertension. Reducing alcohol from heavy to moderate levels reduces SBP by 5-10 mmHg.
foods_to_avoid.recommendation: Ideally avoid; if consumed: maximum 2 standard drinks/day men (14 units/week); 1 drink/day women (7 units/week). Complete abstinence recommended if hypertension is difficult to control.

foods_to_avoid.reason: Promote endothelial dysfunction and atherosclerosis; increase LDL cholesterol; reduce HDL; combined cardiovascular risk with hypertension is multiplicative.
examples: Coconut oil (high in saturated fat despite popular claims)

foods_to_avoid.reason: Fructose (in HFCS and sucrose) directly raises BP by increasing uric acid and activating RAAS; promotes obesity (hypertension risk factor); insulin resistance; dyslipidaemia. NHANES data links sugar-sweetened beverages with higher BP independently of weight.
examples: Soft drinks (cola, lemon sodas, fruit drinks)

foods_to_avoid.reason: Caffeine acutely raises BP by 3-4 mmHg within 30-60 minutes through sympathomimetic effects. Regular drinkers develop partial tolerance but still show acute pressor responses. People who are non-habitual drinkers or genetically slow caffeine metabolisers show larger BP rises.
foods_to_avoid.recommendation: Limit to 1-2 cups of coffee or tea daily; measure BP 1-2 hours after caffeine intake to assess personal response; reduce if BP rises significantly
examples: Strong black tea in large volumes

foods_to_avoid.reason: Glycyrrhizic acid in licorice inhibits the enzyme that inactivates cortisol in the kidney — causes pseudo-hyperaldosteronism: sodium retention, potassium loss, and high BP. Even moderate consumption (50-100g daily for 2 weeks) raises BP significantly.
examples: Some herbal medicines and Ayurvedic preparations

foods_to_avoid.reason: Hidden sources of salt that are often overlooked but can substantially increase daily sodium intake.
examples: Instant spice mixes and stock cubes

foods_to_avoid.reason: Processed meats contain high sodium (preservation) and nitrate preservatives; red meat high in saturated fat and arachidonic acid; promotes hypertension, atherosclerosis, and kidney damage
examples: Processed meats: sausages, bacon, salami, deli meats
Organ meats (liver, kidney — also high in cholesterol)

sample_meal_plan.note: This DASH-inspired low-sodium, high-potassium anti-hypertensive meal plan is a general guideline. Individual needs vary based on comorbidities (diabetes, CKD, heart failure). Consult a registered dietitian for personalized guidance. All cooking should use minimal added salt — use herbs and spices for flavoring.
sample_meal_plan.early_morning: Warm water with lemon (alkalizing; Vitamin C) + 7-8 soaked almonds and 4-5 walnuts (unsalted) + 250mL fresh beetroot juice or pomegranate juice
sample_meal_plan.breakfast: Oatmeal with banana, flaxseeds, and fresh berries (no added sugar or salt) + 1 cup low-fat yogurt OR Whole wheat vegetable upma (no salt — use lemon and herbs) + 1 glass skimmed buttermilk + 2 cups green tea
sample_meal_plan.mid_morning: Fresh fruit (1 orange and 5-6 strawberries) OR hibiscus/roselle herbal tea + 1 banana
sample_meal_plan.lunch: Brown rice or 2 whole wheat chapati (no salt in dough) + 1 bowl dal (lentil soup — minimal salt) + spinach sabzi or methi sabzi with garlic + 1 medium baked sweet potato + 1 cup low-fat curd + cucumber and tomato salad with lemon dressing (no salt)
sample_meal_plan.evening_snack: Unsalted roasted pumpkin seeds or mixed nuts (almonds, walnuts) + 1 cup hibiscus or green tea OR fresh coconut water
sample_meal_plan.dinner: Grilled fish (salmon/mackerel) OR paneer with vegetables + 2 whole wheat chapati + stir-fried kale/spinach with garlic and olive oil + 1 cup dal + tomato and avocado salad
sample_meal_plan.before_bed: Warm skimmed milk with 1/2 tsp turmeric and a pinch of black pepper (golden milk) OR chamomile tea

special_dietary_notes: SODIUM RESTRICTION is the single most important dietary intervention — target <2g sodium per day; start by eliminating added salt at the table and cooking with herbs instead
Weight loss is second most powerful lifestyle intervention — each kg lost reduces SBP by 1-2 mmHg; 10% body weight loss can reduce SBP by 10 mmHg
DASH diet reduces SBP by 8-14 mmHg and DBP by 4-6 mmHg — comparable to starting one antihypertensive drug
Dietary potassium (3,500-4,700 mg/day from food) reduces SBP by 3-8 mmHg — especially important when taking non-potassium-sparing diuretics
Patients on ACEi/ARBs and spironolactone should AVOID potassium supplements and excessive potassium foods — risk of dangerous hyperkalaemia
Patients on warfarin: sudden large increases in vitamin K-rich green vegetables (spinach, kale) can alter INR — maintain consistent intake rather than eliminate
Alcohol — even modest reductions (e.g., from 3-4 drinks to 1-2/day) produce meaningful BP reductions
Caffeine — assess personal BP response; some patients show marked caffeine sensitivity
Consider Mediterranean diet as a practical, culturally adaptable framework that incorporates most DASH principles while also reducing overall cardiovascular risk

physical_activity.overview: Regular aerobic exercise is the most powerful single lifestyle intervention for hypertension — reduces SBP by 5-8 mmHg and DBP by 3-5 mmHg in hypertensive patients. Equivalent to the effect of one antihypertensive drug.

examples: Brisk walking (30-45 min most days — most accessible; ideal for all ages)
recommended_exercises.frequency: At least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity per week (30 min × 5 days minimum) or 75 minutes vigorous-intensity
recommended_exercises.intensity: Moderate: talking is possible but slightly breathless; aim for 50-70% of maximum heart rate (220 minus age)

recommended_exercises.frequency: 2-3 days per week; 8-10 exercises; 8-12 repetitions each
recommended_exercises.note: Avoid Valsalva manoeuvre (breath-holding and straining) — causes acute spike in BP; always breathe out during exertion

recommended_exercises.frequency: 3 sessions per week; 4 × 2-min contractions at 30-50% MVC with 3 min rest
recommended_exercises.bp_reduction: Most recently published meta-analysis shows isometric resistance training reduces SBP by 8-10 mmHg — greater than aerobic exercise
recommended_exercises.note: 2023 British Journal of Sports Medicine meta-analysis showing isometric exercises most effective for BP reduction

recommended_exercises.frequency: Daily if possible; at least 3 times per week
recommended_exercises.bp_reduction: SBP reduction: 3-5 mmHg; additional stress reduction benefit
recommended_exercises.specific_pranayama: Anulom Vilom (alternate nostril breathing); Bhramari; slow deep breathing (6 breaths/min for 15 min); slow breathing reduces SBP by 3-4 mmHg

precautions: Always warm up 5-10 minutes before exercise; cool down 5-10 minutes after
Check BP before exercise — if SBP >180 or DBP >110 mmHg, do NOT exercise; treat BP first
Avoid very heavy weight lifting and Valsalva manoeuvre (extreme breath-holding and straining)
Exercise in cool environment — avoid extreme heat (worsens hypotension risk)
Stay well hydrated before and during exercise
Report chest pain, palpitations, dizziness, or unusual breathlessness during exercise immediately — stop and seek medical attention
Exercise-induced hypotension is possible after antihypertensives — rise slowly after exercise, especially with beta-blockers, alpha-blockers, or vasodilators

weight_management.evidence: Every kg of weight lost reduces SBP by 1-2 mmHg and DBP by 0.5-1 mmHg. 10% body weight reduction can reduce SBP by 10 mmHg. Abdominal obesity (>102cm waist in men; >88cm in women) is particularly harmful.
weight_management.target_bmi: 18.5-24.9 kg/m² for most adults; waist circumference <102cm men, <88cm women
strategies: Calorie-controlled diet with 500-750 calorie daily deficit for 0.5-1 kg/week weight loss
DASH diet — naturally promotes weight loss through high fibre and low calorie density
Reduce ultra-processed foods, sugary beverages, refined carbohydrates
Mindful eating — eat slowly, avoid distracted eating, smaller portions on smaller plates
Professional dietitian/nutritionist support for structured weight loss programme

smoking_cessation.importance: Smoking causes acute sharp BP elevation (3-5 mmHg per cigarette); accelerates atherosclerosis exponentially when combined with hypertension; is the most important preventable cause of cardiovascular mortality; dramatically reduces antihypertensive medication efficacy
smoking_cessation.bp_effect: Though smoking acutely raises BP, the chronic BP-lowering effect of quitting is modest — the primary benefit is dramatic reduction in overall cardiovascular risk (MI, stroke, peripheral artery disease, aortic aneurysm)
strategies: Brief physician advice to quit at every consultation increases quit rates
Nicotine Replacement Therapy (NRT): patches, gum, lozenges, inhaler
Varenicline (Champix/Chantix) — most effective pharmacotherapy; doubles quit rates
Bupropion (Zyban) — effective; monitor BP (slight pressor effect)
Behavioural support: individual or group counselling

stress_management.evidence: Chronic psychological stress elevates BP through sustained sympathetic activation and cortisol release. Stress management interventions reduce SBP by 3-4 mmHg. Job strain and social isolation are independent hypertension risk factors.
techniques: Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) — 8-week structured programme; reduces SBP by 4-7 mmHg; reduces anxiety and cortisol
Slow, deep breathing exercises — 6 breaths per minute for 15 minutes daily; activates parasympathetic nervous system; reduces SBP 3-4 mmHg
Transcendental Meditation (TM) and other forms of meditation — AHA scientific statement acknowledges TM as having reasonable evidence for BP reduction
Progressive Muscle Relaxation (PMR) — systematic tension-release of muscle groups; reduces sympathetic tone
Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) — for anxiety and stress-related hypertension
Yoga and pranayama — dual benefit of physical activity and stress reduction
Social connection and support — isolation is a cardiovascular risk factor
Adequate sleep — address sleep disorders; sleep restriction elevates BP

sleep_hygiene.importance: Insufficient sleep (<6 hours/night) and poor sleep quality raise BP; increase risk of hypertension by 20-32%. Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is both caused by and causes hypertension — bidirectional relationship. Non-dipping nocturnal BP pattern (BP does not fall 10-20% during sleep) is associated with worse cardiovascular outcomes.
recommendations: Target 7-8 hours of good quality sleep per night
Consistent sleep-wake schedule — same bedtime and wake time daily
No screens (phones, tablets, TV) for 1 hour before bed (blue light disrupts melatonin)
Avoid large meals and alcohol close to bedtime
Screen for OSA in: obese patients, non-dippers on ABPM, those with witnessed snoring and excessive daytime sleepiness — CPAP therapy for OSA reduces SBP by 3-10 mmHg

home_bp_monitoring.importance: Home blood pressure monitoring (HBPM) improves BP control, identifies white coat hypertension, detects masked hypertension, and improves medication adherence.
technique: Use a validated upper arm automated oscillometric device (wrist devices less accurate)
Sit quietly for 5 minutes before measuring
Support arm at heart level on table
Take 2 readings morning (before medication and breakfast) and 2 readings evening, for 7 consecutive days
Discard day 1 readings; average the rest
Home BP threshold: ≥135/85 mmHg = hypertension (lower than office threshold of 140/90)
Share readings diary with healthcare provider at each consultation

hypertension_monitoring_plan.note: Blood pressure is best monitored with a validated home BP monitor. Consistent monitoring allows early detection of uncontrolled BP before complications occur. The following zones guide when to take action.

green_zone.bp_criteria: SBP 110-139 mmHg AND DBP 70-89 mmHg (home readings); target <130/80 in high-risk patients
green_zone.symptoms: No symptoms; feeling well; medication tolerated
green_zone.action: Continue current medications and lifestyle changes. Home monitoring twice daily, 3 days per week. GP or cardiologist review every 3-6 months. Annual blood tests (renal function, electrolytes, lipids, glucose). Annual urine ACR. Annual ECG.

yellow_zone.bp_criteria: SBP 140-179 mmHg OR DBP 90-109 mmHg (average of multiple home readings)
yellow_zone.symptoms: Possible headache, dizziness; otherwise may be asymptomatic
yellow_zone.action: Contact GP or cardiologist within 1-2 weeks. Review medication adherence and lifestyle factors. Medication dose adjustment or additional drug may be required. Recheck home BP readings twice daily. Reduce salt and alcohol. Increase physical activity. Repeat blood tests if not done recently.

urgency_no_symptoms.definition: BP ≥180/120 WITHOUT any symptoms of target organ damage
urgency_no_symptoms.symptoms: No headache, no chest pain, no visual change, no neurological symptoms
urgency_no_symptoms.action: Contact GP or cardiologist SAME DAY or go to urgent care. Additional oral antihypertensive may be prescribed. Rest; reduce salt; avoid strenuous exercise. Recheck BP in 1-2 hours. Do NOT reduce BP too rapidly with self-medication.

emergency_with_symptoms.definition: BP ≥180/120 WITH any symptoms of target organ damage
emergency_with_symptoms.symptoms: Any of: severe headache, visual disturbance or vision loss, chest pain, shortness of breath, confusion, focal weakness or speech difficulty, severe nausea/vomiting, back or chest tearing pain
emergency_with_symptoms.action: CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES (102/112 India; 999 UK; 911 USA) IMMEDIATELY. This is a hypertensive emergency. Do NOT drive yourself. Lie down, rest, loosen clothing. Do NOT take extra doses of antihypertensive without medical guidance — uncontrolled BP reduction is dangerous.

complications.name: Ischaemic Stroke
complications.description: Hypertension is the leading modifiable risk factor for stroke — accounts for 50-60% of all strokes. Elevated BP causes atherosclerosis of large cerebral arteries and lipohyalinosis of small penetrating arteries (lacunar infarcts). Every 10 mmHg increase in SBP raises stroke risk by 30-40%.
complications.severity: Potentially life-threatening; major cause of long-term disability
