complications.prevention: Each 5 mmHg SBP reduction reduces stroke risk by 34%

complications.name: Haemorrhagic Stroke (Intracerebral Haemorrhage)
complications.description: High BP causes rupture of cerebral microaneurysms (Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms) and hypertensive arteriopathy. ICH carries much higher acute mortality than ischaemic stroke (up to 40%). Hypertension accounts for >60% of ICH cases.

complications.name: Transient Ischaemic Attack (TIA)
complications.description: Brief episode of focal neurological deficit (lasting <24 hours, typically <1 hour) without infarction. Important warning sign — 10-15% risk of stroke within 90 days, highest in first 48 hours. Urgently investigate and treat. Hypertension is the most common cause.

complications.name: Hypertensive Encephalopathy
complications.description: Severe acute BP elevation causing cerebral oedema, dysfunction of cerebral autoregulation, and posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES). Presents with severe headache, nausea, visual disturbance, confusion, and seizures. Rare but requires immediate treatment.

complications.name: Vascular Dementia and Cognitive Decline
complications.description: Chronic hypertension damages cerebral small vessels (cerebral small vessel disease — SVD), causing white matter lesions (leukoaraiosis), lacunar infarcts, and progressive cognitive decline. Hypertension is the leading modifiable cause of vascular dementia. Even midlife hypertension increases late-life dementia risk by 50-100%.

complications.name: Left Ventricular Hypertrophy (LVH)
complications.description: Hypertrophic remodelling of the left ventricle in response to chronically elevated afterload. LVH is a precursor to heart failure, arrhythmias, sudden death, and MI. LVH on ECG triples cardiovascular event risk. Regression of LVH is achievable with effective antihypertensive treatment.
complications.severity: Moderate; marker of advanced target organ damage

complications.name: Myocardial Infarction (Heart Attack)
complications.description: Hypertension accelerates coronary atherosclerosis and increases myocardial oxygen demand. Major independent risk factor for MI — doubles MI risk. Combined with smoking or diabetes, risk is multiplicative.

complications.name: Heart Failure — Both HFrEF and HFpEF
complications.description: Hypertension is the leading cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) — predominantly diastolic dysfunction from LVH and myocardial fibrosis. Also contributes to HFrEF when combined with ischaemic disease. Estimated 68% of heart failure cases are attributable to hypertension.

complications.name: Atrial Fibrillation (AF)
complications.description: Hypertension-induced LVH and left atrial enlargement — the most common cause of AF. AF independently increases stroke risk 5-fold. Hypertension management is the cornerstone of AF prevention.

complications.name: Aortic Aneurysm and Dissection
complications.description: Chronic high BP causes aortic wall stress and medial degeneration — promoting aortic aneurysm formation and dissection. Aortic dissection (type A or B) is a catastrophic complication — requires emergency surgery (type A) or IV antihypertensives (type B). Most abdominal aortic aneurysms are complicated by hypertension.

complications.name: Hypertensive Nephrosclerosis and Chronic Kidney Disease
complications.description: Elevated glomerular capillary pressure and ischaemia from afferent arteriolar constriction cause progressive nephrosclerosis (glomerulosclerosis, tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis). Hypertension is the second leading cause of end-stage renal disease (ESRD) requiring dialysis after diabetes. Hypertension and CKD mutually worsen each other — vicious cycle.

complications.name: Microalbuminuria and Proteinuria
complications.description: Earliest marker of hypertensive renal damage. Microalbuminuria (ACR 3-30 mg/mmol) independently predicts cardiovascular and renal events. Progression from microalbuminuria to macroalbuminuria to declining GFR occurs over years if untreated.
complications.severity: Mild initially; marker of significant systemic vascular damage

complications.name: Hypertensive Retinopathy
complications.description: Fundoscopic changes in retinal arteries reflecting systemic vascular damage: Keith-Wagener-Barker Grade I (arterial narrowing, silver/copper wire appearance) → Grade II (AV nipping — artery compresses vein at crossing) → Grade III (flame haemorrhages, cotton wool spots) → Grade IV (papilloedema = hypertensive emergency). Grades III-IV represent hypertensive emergencies.
complications.severity: Grade I-II: mild; Grade III: emergency; Grade IV: emergency with vision threat

complications.name: Retinal Artery and Vein Occlusion
complications.description: Hypertension is the leading risk factor for central and branch retinal artery and vein occlusions — causing sudden visual loss in the affected eye. Central retinal artery occlusion is effectively a 'stroke of the eye' — requires immediate treatment within hours.
complications.severity: Severe — can cause permanent visual loss

complications.name: Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD)
complications.description: Hypertension accelerates atherosclerosis in peripheral arteries — causing intermittent claudication (calf pain on walking), rest pain, and critical limb ischaemia. Combined with smoking, PAD risk is dramatically increased.

complications.name: Erectile Dysfunction
complications.description: Penile vasculature highly sensitive to hypertensive vascular damage and endothelial dysfunction. Affects 40-50% of hypertensive men. Also worsened by antihypertensive medications (thiazides, beta-blockers). ACEi/ARBs and CCBs are preferred in hypertensive patients with ED.

complications.name: Pre-eclampsia and Eclampsia
complications.description: Severe hypertension in pregnancy with multi-organ involvement (proteinuria, hepatic, neurological, haematological). Eclampsia = pre-eclampsia + seizures. Leading cause of maternal mortality globally. Pre-eclampsia affects 2-8% of pregnancies. Requires immediate delivery if severe or at term.

complications.name: HELLP Syndrome
complications.description: Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets — severe variant of pre-eclampsia. Medical emergency requiring immediate delivery.

key_points: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy affect 10% of pregnancies and are a leading cause of maternal and perinatal mortality worldwide
ACE inhibitors and ARBs are ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy — cause fetal renal agenesis, oligohydramnios, IUGR, and neonatal death. Stop immediately if pregnancy detected or planned.
Safe antihypertensives in pregnancy: Methyldopa (first-line; 50+ year safety record), Labetalol (oral and IV), Nifedipine SR/LA (oral), Hydralazine (IV for emergencies)
Treatment threshold in pregnancy: SBP ≥150 mmHg or DBP ≥100 mmHg (to prevent maternal stroke); avoid lowering BP too aggressively (<130/80) — fetal growth impairment
Gestational hypertension (after 20 weeks without proteinuria): monitor closely; 25% develop pre-eclampsia

Pre-eclampsia: new onset hypertension + proteinuria after 20 weeks; screen with uterine artery Doppler, PIGF, sFlt-1 from 11-14 weeks; low-dose aspirin 150 mg at night from 12-36 weeks reduces pre-eclampsia risk by 62% in high-risk women
IV Magnesium Sulfate: essential for seizure prevention and treatment in pre-eclampsia/eclampsia; reduces maternal morbidity and mortality
Eclampsia: tonic-clonic seizures in a pregnant/postpartum woman — IV MgSO4 + antihypertensives + emergency delivery
Postpartum: hypertension may persist or worsen in first 5 days after delivery; monitor closely; continue antihypertensives; NSAIDs may worsen BP post-partum — avoid
Women with pre-eclampsia are at 3-4x increased lifetime cardiovascular risk — long-term cardiovascular follow-up essential after pregnancy
Most common chronic condition in elderly — affects >70% of adults over 70 years
Isolated systolic hypertension (ISH) predominates — from aortic stiffening; wide pulse pressure (>60 mmHg) is an independent cardiovascular risk marker
Treatment benefit is GREATER in elderly than young — absolute risk reduction is higher despite same relative risk reduction
SPRINT trial showed intensive BP target (<120 mmHg systolic) beneficial even in adults >75 years; but must balance against adverse effects

Orthostatic hypotension is a major concern — fall-related fractures are a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in elderly hypertensives. Measure standing BP; start medications at lowest doses; avoid polypharmacy
Dementia prevention: reducing BP in midlife (40-65 years) significantly reduces dementia risk; SPRINT MIND trial showed intensive BP control reduces mild cognitive impairment
Preferred drugs in elderly: dihydropyridine CCBs (amlodipine) and thiazide-like diuretics (chlorthalidone, indapamide); avoid high-dose diuretics and beta-blockers as first-line
Multiple comorbidities and polypharmacy: review medications regularly; drug interactions common; simplify regimen where possible; fixed-dose combinations improve adherence
Frail elderly: BP targets may be less aggressive; individualise — balance benefits vs risk of falls and adverse effects
Secondary hypertension much more common in children than adults — investigate all hypertensive children for renal, endocrine, and vascular causes
Most common secondary causes in children: renal parenchymal disease (most common), coarctation of aorta, renal artery stenosis
Diagnosis requires age-, sex-, and height-specific BP percentile tables (for children <13 years); adult thresholds used for adolescents ≥13 years
Paediatric hypertension definition: average SBP or DBP ≥95th percentile for age, sex, height on 3 separate occasions
Adolescent hypertension is increasingly linked to obesity — weight loss is primary treatment; ACE inhibitors or ARBs are preferred pharmacological options in children
Lifestyle modification — weight loss, salt restriction, physical activity — is first-line for mild hypertension in children and adolescents
Cardiac, renal, and retinal assessment for end-organ damage in paediatric hypertension
50% of people with type 2 diabetes have hypertension; coexistence dramatically increases cardiovascular and renal risk
BP target in diabetes: <130/80 mmHg (ACC/AHA, NICE) — stricter than in non-diabetic hypertension
ACE inhibitors or ARBs are FIRST-LINE in diabetic hypertension — specifically reduce diabetic nephropathy progression (independent of BP lowering); required if any proteinuria present
SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) have dual benefit — glucose lowering AND modest BP lowering AND proven cardiovascular and renal protection in diabetic hypertensives
Monitor for hypoglycaemia — beta-blockers blunt tachycardia (warning sign of hypoglycaemia); sweating preserved; use selective beta-blockers only if indicated
ACE inhibitors or ARBs are mandatory first-line treatment in hypertensive CKD — reduce proteinuria and slow progression of renal disease beyond their BP-lowering effect (renoprotective)
BP target in CKD with proteinuria: <130/80 mmHg
Monitor renal function and potassium 1-2 weeks after starting ACEi/ARB — acceptable creatinine rise up to 30%; stop if rise >50%
Thiazides lose effectiveness when eGFR <30 — switch to loop diuretics (furosemide, torasemide)
Avoid NSAIDs — nephrotoxic and raise BP
Anaemia of CKD worsens cardiac workload — treat with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents and iron
Higher prevalence of hypertension and more severe forms; lower renin levels mean RAAS blockers (ACEi, ARBs) are LESS effective as monotherapy
CCBs (amlodipine) and thiazide diuretics preferred first-line as monotherapy
ACEi and ARBs effective when combined with CCB or thiazide — add as second drug
Higher risk of ACEi-induced angioedema in Black patients
Genetic salt sensitivity higher — sodium restriction particularly important
Higher risk of end-organ damage at any given BP level

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Flu infection significantly increases cardiovascular events — multiple studies show flu vaccination reduces MI risk by 15-45% in hypertensive patients. Acute infection raises BP and triggers cardiovascular complications. Priority vaccination for all patients with hypertension.

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: PCV20 or PCV15 single dose then PPSV23 1 year later; booster at 65 if given earlier
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Pneumococcal pneumonia is a significant cardiovascular trigger; patients with hypertension and target organ damage (especially heart failure, CKD) at high risk for severe pneumococcal disease and complications

COVID-19 infection substantially raises BP and dramatically increases risk of myocarditis, stroke, and heart failure in hypertensive patients. Hypertension is a major risk factor for severe COVID-19 outcomes. Vaccination strongly recommended.

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: 2 doses, 2-6 months apart; for adults ≥50 years
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Shingles (herpes zoster) acutely raises BP and dramatically increases short-term risk of MI and stroke in the weeks after infection. Shingrix vaccination reduces shingles risk by 97% in adults 50-69 and 91% in adults ≥70.
Routine adult immunisation; bacterial infections including whooping cough can trigger acute cardiovascular events in patients with underlying hypertension and heart disease
Hypertensive patients with CKD are at increased risk of hepatitis B — CKD impairs immune response. Important if hypertension has led to significant renal impairment or pre-dialysis stage.

when_to_see_doctor: Newly measured BP ≥140/90 mmHg on two or more separate occasions — arrange formal hypertension assessment
Home BP readings consistently ≥135/85 mmHg — warrants medical evaluation
Persistent headache — especially occipital (back of head) on waking — combined with high BP
Dizziness, visual disturbances, or palpitations with high blood pressure readings
Starting a new medication that may raise BP — NSAIDs, oral contraceptive pill, decongestants, steroids
BP uncontrolled on current antihypertensive medications — medication adjustment needed
Side effects from antihypertensive drugs — ACEi cough, ankle swelling, dizziness, fatigue
Planning a pregnancy or discovered pregnant while on antihypertensives — ACEi and ARBs MUST be stopped
New symptoms of target organ damage: chest pain, breathlessness, palpitations, visual changes, swollen ankles, reduced urine output
Annual review — even if BP is well controlled: blood tests, urine ACR, ECG, cardiovascular risk assessment
Blood pressure falling too low (symptomatic hypotension — dizziness on standing, fainting) on medication
Blood pressure that was well controlled becoming difficult to control — possible secondary cause or medication interaction
Discovery of a new health condition that may affect blood pressure management (CKD, diabetes, heart failure)
emergency_signs: Sudden severe 'thunderclap' headache — worst headache ever experienced — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES: possible subarachnoid haemorrhage or hypertensive emergency

Sudden weakness, numbness, or paralysis of face, arm, or leg (especially one-sided) combined with high BP — STROKE — FAST: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services
Sudden slurred speech, aphasia (word-finding difficulty), or facial drooping — STROKE
Sudden loss of vision in one or both eyes with high BP — hypertensive emergency or retinal artery occlusion
Severe tearing or ripping chest pain spreading to the back — possible aortic dissection — IMMEDIATE EMERGENCY
Sudden severe chest pain, pressure, or tightness with shortness of breath — possible heart attack (MI)
Acute breathlessness at rest, pink frothy sputum, coughing while lying flat — acute pulmonary oedema from hypertensive heart failure
Confusion, altered consciousness, agitation, or seizures with very high BP — hypertensive encephalopathy or intracerebral haemorrhage
Seizures in a pregnant woman — ECLAMPSIA — life-threatening obstetric emergency
BP ≥180/120 mmHg WITH any of: severe headache, vision changes, chest pain, breathlessness, or neurological symptoms — HYPERTENSIVE EMERGENCY — call ambulance

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is hypertension and why is it called the 'silent killer'?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Hypertension (high blood pressure) means the force of blood pressing against artery walls is consistently too high — ≥140/90 mmHg. It's called the silent killer because most people (over 80%) have no symptoms, even with significantly high readings. Without regular BP checks, many only discover they have hypertension after it causes a serious complication — heart attack, stroke, kidney failure, or heart failure. This is why regular BP screening is so important.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What causes high blood pressure?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: In 90-95% of cases, hypertension is 'primary' (essential) — no single cause but results from complex interactions of genetics, age, lifestyle (high salt diet, obesity, inactivity, excess alcohol), and neurohormonal factors. In 5-10% of cases, a specific cause exists (secondary hypertension) — including kidney disease, primary aldosteronism (Conn's syndrome), pheochromocytoma, sleep apnoea, thyroid disorders, medications (NSAIDs, contraceptive pills, steroids), and rarely coarctation of the aorta.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What are the symptoms of high blood pressure?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Hypertension is usually completely asymptomatic — this is what makes it so dangerous. Some people experience occipital headache (back of head, typically in the morning), dizziness, nosebleeds, or visual blurring, but these are unreliable and non-specific. Symptoms only appear with very high BP or with complications. Regular blood pressure measurement is the only way to detect it. Everyone over 18 should have their BP checked at least every 2 years.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the normal blood pressure range?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Normal (optimal): below 120/80 mmHg. High normal: 130-139/85-89 mmHg (lifestyle changes needed). Grade 1 Hypertension: 140-159/90-99 mmHg. Grade 2: 160-179/100-109 mmHg. Grade 3 (severe): ≥180/≥110 mmHg. Hypertensive crisis: >180/>120 mmHg. The first number (systolic) is pressure when heart contracts; the second (diastolic) is pressure when heart relaxes. Both are equally important, but systolic BP is a better predictor of cardiovascular risk in people over 50.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How is hypertension treated?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Treatment combines lifestyle changes and medication. Lifestyle: DASH diet (high in fruits, vegetables, low-fat dairy, low in sodium), sodium restriction (<5g salt/day), weight loss, regular exercise (150+ min/week), alcohol reduction, smoking cessation, and stress management. These alone can reduce BP by 20-30 mmHg. Medications: 4 main first-line drug classes — ACE inhibitors (ramipril, lisinopril), ARBs (losartan, telmisartan), calcium channel blockers (amlodipine), and thiazide diuretics (indapamide, chlorthalidone). Most patients need 2-3 drugs for optimal control.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Do I need to take blood pressure medications for life?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: For primary hypertension, medication is usually lifelong — stopping treatment allows BP to rise again. However, if lifestyle changes result in significant weight loss, sodium restriction, and BP normalization, some patients can reduce or stop medications under medical supervision. Never stop antihypertensive medication without medical guidance — sudden discontinuation can cause rebound hypertensive crisis (especially with clonidine or beta-blockers).

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the DASH diet and does it really lower blood pressure?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) is the most evidence-based dietary strategy for hypertension. It emphasizes: 8-10 servings of fruits and vegetables daily (potassium, magnesium, antioxidants), whole grains, low-fat dairy (calcium), lean proteins, limiting sodium (<5g salt/day), and avoiding saturated fat, red meat, sweets, and sugary beverages. Multiple large clinical trials show DASH diet alone reduces SBP by 8-14 mmHg — equivalent to starting one antihypertensive drug. Combined with sodium restriction, it reduces SBP by up to 20 mmHg.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can reducing salt intake really make a difference?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — dramatically. Sodium restriction is the single most effective dietary change for hypertension. Every 1g/day reduction in sodium reduces SBP by 2-5 mmHg. Reducing from average consumption (4-5g sodium/day = 10-12g salt/day) to the recommended limit (2g sodium = 5g salt/day) can reduce SBP by 5-10 mmHg. The biggest sources of hidden sodium are processed foods, restaurant meals, canned foods, bread, sauces, and pickles — not just table salt. Reading food labels and cooking fresh food with herbs instead of salt is the most effective approach.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Are ACE inhibitors and ARBs the same thing?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Both block the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and have similar BP-lowering and organ-protective effects. ACE inhibitors (ramipril, lisinopril, perindopril) block the enzyme that produces angiotensin II. ARBs (losartan, telmisartan, candesartan) block the angiotensin receptor directly. Key difference: ACE inhibitors cause dry cough in 10-20% of patients (from bradykinin accumulation) — ARBs do not cause cough and are used as replacement. They must NEVER be combined — doubles AKI and hyperkalaemia risk. Both are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is a hypertensive emergency and how is it different from hypertensive urgency?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Both involve very high BP (usually >180/120 mmHg). Hypertensive URGENCY: severely elevated BP WITHOUT acute target organ damage — treated with oral medications and gradual BP reduction over 24-48 hours; usually outpatient. Hypertensive EMERGENCY: severely elevated BP WITH acute target organ damage — brain (encephalopathy, stroke), heart (MI, pulmonary oedema), aorta (dissection), kidneys (AKI), eyes (papilloedema), or eclampsia. Requires IMMEDIATE emergency services call, ICU admission, and IV antihypertensive medications. Do NOT lower BP too rapidly — brain and heart ischaemia can worsen.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is hypertension in pregnancy dangerous?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — hypertensive disorders of pregnancy affect 10% of pregnancies and are a leading cause of maternal and fetal death worldwide. Severe forms — pre-eclampsia (high BP + proteinuria after 20 weeks) and eclampsia (with seizures) — require urgent delivery and IV magnesium sulfate. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy — they cause fatal fetal abnormalities. Safe medications include methyldopa, labetalol, and nifedipine SR. Women with a history of pre-eclampsia have 3-4x higher lifetime cardiovascular risk.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Why do I need regular blood tests on antihypertensive medication?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Different antihypertensives require different monitoring: ACEi and ARBs can raise potassium (hyperkalaemia — heart rhythm problems) and impair kidney function — renal function and potassium checked 1-4 weeks after starting and annually. Diuretics (thiazides and loop diuretics) can lower potassium and sodium — electrolytes monitored. Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone) can cause dangerous potassium elevation — especially with ACEi/ARBs. All patients benefit from annual blood tests: renal function, electrolytes, lipids, glucose, and urine ACR (for kidney damage detection).

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can stress cause high blood pressure?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Stress causes acute BP elevation through adrenaline and cortisol release — this is the 'flight or fight' response. Chronic psychosocial stress (job strain, financial pressure, relationship problems, bereavement) sustains sympathetic nervous system overactivation, contributing to persistent hypertension. Regular stress causes approximately 3-5 mmHg chronic BP elevation. Stress management through mindfulness meditation, yoga, slow deep breathing (6 breaths/min), and CBT can reduce SBP by 3-7 mmHg and should be a component of hypertension management.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What foods should I eat to lower my blood pressure?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Focus on: (1) Potassium-rich foods — bananas, sweet potato, spinach, avocado, coconut water, dal; (2) Nitrate-rich vegetables — beetroot juice, spinach, kale, rocket; (3) Low-fat dairy — skimmed milk, yogurt, buttermilk; (4) Fatty fish — salmon, mackerel, sardines; (5) Dark berries — blueberries, pomegranate; (6) Garlic (raw or extract); (7) Unsalted nuts — walnuts, almonds; (8) Dark chocolate (≥70% cocoa); (9) Green tea; (10) Hibiscus tea. Combine these in a DASH-pattern diet and restrict sodium to <5g salt/day.
